segments.say: So far we have looked at how a dream is built, and how it can seem so solid while it lasts. Now let's turn to something quieter, which is what a night of dreaming might do for the way you feel the next day. Some of the most interesting research in sleep science asks whether dreams are only a show, or whether they are part of a kind of overnight housekeeping for your emotions.

You may know this from your own life. Something upsetting happens on a Tuesday evening, and it feels sharp and heavy. You sleep, perhaps you dream, perhaps you don't remember. And by Wednesday morning, the same memory is still there, but it has lost some of its sting. People have said for centuries that things look different in the morning. Scientists wondered whether that old saying describes something real.

show.sub: Last night's feeling, this morning's calm

segments.say: The question is a careful one. It is not whether dreams can cure you of anything, because nobody is claiming that. It is whether the sleeping brain handles the feeling attached to a memory differently from the facts of the memory, and whether the dreaming stage of sleep has a role in that.

show.title: The question for this chapter
items: Does sleep change how a memory feels?
Does dreaming play a part?
What does the evidence actually show?

segments.say: In 2009, Matthew Walker and Els van der Helm, at the University of California, Berkeley, published a long review of the research on sleep and emotion. They gathered findings from brain imaging, from experiments on memory, and from studies of people with mood problems, and they proposed a framework to tie them together. Their title ended with a question mark, and that is worth noticing.

show.who: Matthew Walker & Els van der Helm
show.what: Overnight therapy? The role of sleep in emotional brain processing

segments.say: It is a good habit to notice a question mark in a title. Scientists use one when they are proposing, and not yet proving. Walker and van der Helm were not announcing that sleep is a form of therapy. They were asking whether it might act a little like one, and they laid out the evidence for and against, so that other researchers could test it. That spirit of careful curiosity is the one we will keep for the rest of this chapter.

Their idea has a rather poetic name: sleep to forget and sleep to remember. The proposal is that overnight, and especially during REM sleep, your brain does two things at the same time. It keeps the facts of an emotional experience, what happened, where, and with whom. And it gradually reduces the emotional charge attached to that memory. The story stays. The sting fades.

show.sub: Sleep to remember, sleep to forget

segments.say: The authors point to three features of REM sleep. Emotional regions, including the amygdala, become active again. Theta rhythms may help different regions to share information. And levels of noradrenaline, a chemical linked with stress and alarm, fall very low. That combination, they suggest, could make REM sleep a safe setting in which to revisit an upsetting memory without the full alarm that came with it.

show.title: What REM sleep offers, according to the review
items: Emotional brain regions such as the amygdala are active again
Slow rhythms called theta waves help regions to communicate
Stress-related chemicals are much lower than during waking

segments.say: Think of it as looking at an old photograph of a hard day while sitting in a calm room, instead of living the day again. During the day, a painful memory arrives with a rush of stress. During REM sleep, the proposal goes, the memory can be replayed while the stress chemistry is turned down, and each replay might loosen the emotional grip a little. It is a lovely picture. The question is how well the evidence supports it.

The review leans on several experiments. In one of them, people who had been kept awake for 72 hours did not show the drop in amygdala response to negative pictures that people who had slept did show. In another, a nap study, the improvement in emotional memory followed how much REM sleep people had. These are suggestive results, and the authors present them as such.

show.title: Findings the review draws on
items: After 72 hours without sleep, brain responses to negative pictures were not reduced
People who slept showed a calmer response
In a nap study, emotional memory tracked time spent in REM sleep

segments.say: Imagine a quiet window at night, a lamp left on, the day finally set down. That is where this research places its question. Whatever the sleeping brain does with your feelings, it does it while you are completely unaware, and mostly without a trace by morning. The only evidence we usually have is how the day looks when we wake, and that is exactly why careful experiments matter here.

A memory that is only hours old is still fresh and raw. It has not yet been woven in with everything else you know. One way to picture the idea is that sleep helps with the weaving, linking new experiences to older ones, and putting them in context. Context is calming. A bad afternoon is easier to carry once it has become one event among many in a long life, and not the only thing in the room.

show.cap: Why feelings may need a night

segments.say: There is another strand of this story, one that comes from people going through difficult times, and the researcher most closely linked to it is Rosalind Cartwright.

Rosalind Cartwright was an American sleep researcher, and she asked a very human question. What happens in the dreams of people who are living through a painful life event? To find out, she studied people who were going through a divorce, many of whom were also low in mood, and she recorded their sleep and dreams in the laboratory.

One of her early papers, with the title Broken Dreams, looked at how divorce and depression show up in dream content. A later paper, in 1998, with Cartwright and colleagues, asked whether features of REM sleep and of dreams could help to predict who would recover from depression. The project was to ask whether the night, and not only the day, could tell us how a person was coping.

show.what: Broken dreams: a study of the effects of divorce and depression on dream content

segments.say: As summaries of her work describe it, there was an interesting pattern. People who dreamed about the person they were separating from, and who felt something in those dreams, tended to be more likely to have recovered from low mood when they were followed up later. People who left that person out of their dreams seemed less likely to have done so. It is important to read this carefully.

A link between two things is not the same as one causing the other. It may be that people who were already coping well were the ones whose dreams could face the hard subject. Or it may be that the dreams helped. The research cannot easily separate these. What it does suggest is gentler than the old fear that a sad dream is a bad sign. A dream that touches a sore spot may sometimes be part of the work of mending.

show.title: What this pattern does and does not say
items: It is a link, not proof of cause
Dreams may reflect progress rather than create it
Painful dreams are not a sign of harm
Summaries of the work leave out many details

segments.say: Cartwright herself came to describe dreaming as something like a mood regulation system, an idea that fits neatly with the Walker and van der Helm framework. Both point in the same direction. During sleep, the brain may be working on feelings that the waking day left unfinished. Yet both are careful to say that this is a theory, and that the details are still being tested.

show.sub: A possible role, not a certainty

segments.say: Here are four words you may like to keep. The amygdala is a small region deep in the brain that is closely involved in emotion. Noradrenaline is a chemical linked with stress and alarm. REM sleep is the stage of the night when vivid dreams are most common. And theta waves are slow rhythms that may help distant regions of the brain to share information.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Amygdala: a brain region involved in emotion
Noradrenaline: a chemical linked with stress
REM sleep: the stage with the most vivid dreams
Theta waves: slow rhythms that link brain regions

segments.say: It is worth being honest about the limits here, because this is a subject where a pleasing story can run well ahead of the evidence.

show.title: What we do not know yet

segments.say: Walker and van der Helm call their model a tentative framework, and they say that many of its predictions have not yet been tested. Most of the experiments they describe used negative or arousing pictures, so we know much less about positive emotions. They also note that some findings do not fit, such as a study in which pictures were rated as more unpleasant after sleep, and they say this puzzle remains open.

These are the questions researchers still argue about. One is whether the emotional effects come from the biology of REM sleep, or from the content of the dream, or from both. The review itself says it cannot rule out a role for dream content beyond the physiology. Another is why some people wake from a night of dreams feeling worse, not better. Nobody yet has a settled answer to that.

show.title: Open questions in this field
items: Is it REM sleep itself or the dreams that matter?
How much does the effect depend on the person?
Do the effects last for days, or only overnight?
Why do some nights seem to make things worse?

segments.say: So how should we hold all this? Probably somewhere in the middle. It is unlikely that a night of sleep is a miracle cure for sorrow. It is equally unlikely that dreams are meaningless noise. The more modest reading, and the one the evidence best supports, is that sleep, and REM sleep in particular, seems to help the brain keep what matters about an experience while easing some of its emotional edge.

If you like, try a small experiment of noticing, and not of changing anything. On a day when something has bothered you, take note of how it feels in the evening. Then take note again the next morning. You don't need numbers, only a sense of it. Many people find that the morning version is a little softer.

We should keep this simple. If something has weighed on you, it is not strange for it to feel lighter after you have slept. If you have an upsetting dream, it does not mean that something is broken. And if a low mood or bad dreams stay with you for a long time, that is a good reason to talk to a doctor or someone you trust, because this chapter is a story about science and not a treatment.

show.title: What this might mean for you
items: Hard days may feel different after a night's sleep
An upsetting dream does not mean something is wrong
Sleep and mood seem closely linked
Persistent distress deserves real support

segments.say: Their phrase captures the whole idea in half a dozen words. Remember the facts, forget the sting. Whether the brain really manages that every night is still being studied, but it is a hopeful way of looking at what happens while we are away.

show.text: Sleep to remember and sleep to forget

segments.say: Before we move on, let's rest on one simple thought. Your brain does not switch off when you do. While you lie still, it is replaying, sorting and linking, and some of that work may be about how you feel.

If you have ever had a bad night of dreams and woken tired, it can feel as though sleep has let you down. This research invites a different view. A restless night can still be part of a longer process. Feelings are not settled in one evening, and neither is the brain's work on them. Some of it may happen over many nights, quietly, in the background.

show.cap: A softer view of bad nights
show.sub: Even a restless night does something

segments.say: Everything we have discussed so far has treated the dreamer as a passenger, carried along by a story that the brain tells. But a small number of dreamers have a surprising experience. In the middle of a dream, they realise that they are dreaming, and sometimes they can decide what to do next.

What happens in the brain at that moment, and whether such a dreamer can send a message to the outside world, has been tested with some of the most remarkable experiments in the history of sleep research. So let's see what those researchers found.
